newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to launch major economic reform programme.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to launch major economic reform programme.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif is likely to unveil a sweeping economic reform package on Thursday that will slash taxes, tariffs and public spending to stimulate growth and exports, an official said.
Hafiz Pasha, deputy chairman of the Planning Commission, told Reuters in an interview that Sharif would probably make a major economic policy speech on Thursday.
Sharif's agenda-setting address follows the collapse of an International Monetary Fund standby loan, suspended last week because Pakistan could not meet agreed targets.

Pasha said the package, based on the recommendations of 11 committees set up after Sharif won February 3 elections, would set out a broad policy framework. Details specific to various sectors could wait for the June budget for 1997/98 (July-June).
"The government wants to move in terms of industrial revival and to get the economy going again," said Pasha, who served in the same post in the three-month caretaker administration.
He said IMF-inspired stabilisation measures linked to the standby loan had failed to produce the desired results and the Sharif government aimed for a radical change of direction.
"If we just jacked up tax rates, for example, we were either getting more evasion or the tax base was shrinking because economic activity was being adversely affected," he said.
"The industrial sector was not growing, the inflation rate was still very high, the budget deficit was not coming down and the current account deficit remained very high."
Pasha said tax and tariff rates would be cut to boost growth, but refused to give details ahead of Sharif's speech.
Newspapers on Tuesday said the maximum tariff would be reduced to 45 percent from 65 percent, personal income tax to 36 percent from 38.5 and corporate tax to 38 percent from 46.

They said general sales tax, now applied to imports and manufacturing, would be reduced, but at the same time extended to the retail level. A 10 percent regulatory import duty would be abolished and many tariff concessions withdrawn, but not those provided to the petroleum and power sectors.
The number of public sector corporations would be reduced to 50 from 120 and agricultural income tax would be levied.
Pasha confirmed that measures to broaden the tax and tariff base were vital components of the new strategy.
"It's not pure supply-side economics. It's combined with specific broad-basing measures for revenue generation, which means we will move into agriculture, trade and services."
Pasha promised "massive downsizing" of state corporations, government bodies and financial institutions, which he said could involve the eventual loss of quarter of a million jobs.
He said the workforce of public corporations alone had swollen to about 600,000, a third of which had been added during ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's three-year government.
The cutbacks would be smoothed by golden handshake schemes, early retirement incentives and other sweeteners.

"There might be some transitional costs, but at the end of the day you will have a leaner and far more efficient public sector," he said, adding that the restructuring was necessary to enable "fast-track" privatisation to proceed.
Pasha said he anticipated no difficulty in managing payments on a foreign debt he put at about $35 billion, including short-term borrowing and foreign exchange deposits.

Sharif's debt retirement scheme, which asks Pakistanis to contribute gifts and interest-free or two-year interest-bearing deposits, had helped stabilise liquid foreign reserves at around $1 billion, up from $600 million in late 1996, he added.
Pasha said the IMF would continue to monitor Pakistan's economy and the government would have to show discipline if it was to win access to a medium-term IMF loan later in the year.

"During the transition, we will have to show the kind of commitment to policy reform that is necessary and also broad, macro-economic targets to ensure that we then qualify for an ESAF (enhanced structural adjustment loan)," he said.
"I don't think it's a gamble," he said of Pakistan's impending change of course. "It's an imperative."
